sections.heading: Coming to you through the way you opened
sections.text: Lord Jesus, my great High Priest, you have made a way for someone like me to come near to God and be welcomed. I do not come because I am steady, clean, or deserving. I come because of who you are, because your sacrifice is complete, and because you keep speaking for me before the Father. Help me slow down and really take in the greatness of your person, the sufficiency of your cross, and the strength of your intercession.

scripture_references.connection: This passage grounds Christian confidence to draw near to God in the blood of Jesus and in his priestly work over God's house. It directly supports the prayer's movement from unworthiness to accepted access through Christ.
Hebrews teaches that Jesus saves completely because he always lives to intercede for his people. That is the basis for praying with confidence in his ongoing priestly care.

sections.heading: Bringing my worn-out heart to you
sections.text: When trials wear me down, when responsibilities eat away at my peace, when fear unsettles me, and when my own weakness feels heavy, let me come to you instead of carrying it all alone. Meet me in my need with the kind of peace I cannot manufacture or explain. Teach me that prayer is not an escape from reality, but a place where I bring my real life to you and receive help from you.
theological_themes: peace in Christ amid anxiety and affliction
prayer as coming to Christ for mercy and help

scripture_references.connection: Paul connects anxious circumstances with prayer, thanksgiving, and the guarding peace of God. This supports the prayer's request for peace in the middle of corrosive cares and disturbing fears.
Because Jesus is the sympathetic High Priest, believers are invited to draw near for mercy and timely grace. This fits the prayer's honest approach to Christ under pressure and weakness.

sections.heading: Needing your grace not only to restore me, but to keep me
sections.text: The grace that brought me back to you is the same grace I need to keep going. Preserve me, lead me, guard me, provide for me, and help me. When I look at your people who have gone before me, I am encouraged: they were needy, yet you enriched them; trapped, yet you freed them; tested, yet you carried them through. Let their stories strengthen my hope that you will not abandon me either.

scripture_references.connection: Peter points suffering believers to the God of all grace, who restores and strengthens them after trial. This supports the prayer's claim that grace is needed not only for conversion but for preservation.

After rehearsing the faith of earlier believers, Hebrews calls Christians to endure by looking to Jesus. This grounds the prayer's encouragement from the saints while keeping Christ as the final focus.

sections.heading: Asking from your fullness for every new duty
sections.text: Every new responsibility asks more of me than I already have. But it does not ask more than you can give. You are not poor in mercy, patience, wisdom, courage, or holiness. All fullness is in you. So I come to you again for grace upon grace. Fill the empty places sin has left in me. Stretch my desires so I want more of what is truly good. Make my hopes bolder, not because I trust myself, but because I trust your abundance. Let my dependence on you honor you.

scripture_references.connection: John describes believers receiving from Christ's fullness, grace upon grace. This directly supports asking Christ for repeated and abundant grace for ongoing need.
Paul teaches that all fullness dwells in Christ and that reconciliation comes through him. This supports calling Christ the source from whom every needed grace is supplied.

Paul prays that believers would be strengthened inwardly and filled with the fullness of God. This illuminates the prayer's desire for the emptiness caused by sin to be replenished by God's life and love.

sections.heading: Preparing me for whatever comes next
sections.text: Be with me and make me ready for everything you allow: for seasons that feel bright and easy, and seasons that feel hard and dark; for gains and for losses; for the death of people I love; for days when I cannot see the way forward; for all the changes life brings; and for the final change when my own life in this world comes to an end. In all of it, let me find that your grace is enough for me.

scripture_references.connection: Paul speaks of learning contentment in both abundance and need through the strength Christ supplies. This supports praying to be prepared for both prosperity and adversity.
Christ tells Paul that his grace is sufficient and his power is displayed in weakness. This is the clearest biblical grounding for the prayer's final request that grace meet every need.
Paul describes the final transformation of believers and Christ's victory over death. This supports the prayer's reference to the last great change without treating death as ultimate defeat.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original assumes a strongly Reformed/Puritan view of grace as necessary not only for conversion but also for every step of preservation, obedience, and perseverance. This is broadly biblical, though different Christian traditions may describe the mechanics of grace and perseverance differently.

The phrase about the saints being 'poor and are now rich, bound and are now free, tried and now are victorious' could be read as referring either to believers now in glory or to believers in this life who have experienced deliverance. The adaptation keeps both the encouragement and the focus on Christ's keeping grace without specifying more than the original requires.

The request to be prepared for 'the death of friends' and 'the last great change' reflects a sober Puritan familiarity with mortality. The modern version preserves that directness rather than softening it into vague language about difficulty.
significant_interpretive_choices: I rendered 'fallen creature can approach thee with acceptance' as coming near to God and being welcomed through Christ, to preserve both human unworthiness and divine acceptance without archaic phrasing.
I interpreted 'the grace that restores is necessary to preserve' as a request for continuing grace after conversion, not merely a general request for encouragement.

I kept the concrete range of future circumstances from the original—prosperity, adversity, material loss, bereavement, dark days, life changes, and death—because that sequence is central to the prayer's movement toward Christ's sufficient grace in every condition.

I translated 'the divine Treasury in whom all fullness dwells' into the more natural idea that Christ is not poor in any needed mercy, wisdom, courage, or holiness, while preserving the original claim that all needed grace is found in him.
